alignment.note: Greek ἐπληρώθη (aorist passive of πληρόω, 'was fulfilled') is rendered analytically in Latin by impleta est (perfect passive periphrasis). The Syriac collapses the conjunction and verb into a single form ܘܫܠܡ (root sh-l-m, 'and it was fulfilled/completed'), the same root underlying ܫܠܡܐ 'peace/completion'; hence the Peshitta token 0 carries both the conjunction and the verb.

Greek employs an articular present participle ἡ λέγουσα ('the one saying'), an attributive participial construction; Latin renders this with a relative clause quæ dicit ('which says'). The Syriac ܕܐܡܪ uses the relative/proclitic d- prefix on the verb (root a-m-r), a relative-clause construction parallel to the Latin rather than the Greek participle — a routine syntactic divergence in rendering Greek attributive participles.

The preposition μετά + genitive ('with') and Latin cum + ablative both stand as discrete words, whereas the Syriac fuses the conjunction, preposition, and relative into the proclitic cluster ܕܥܡ (d-ʿm, root d-e-m, 'and-with'); the Syriac orthography agglutinates what Greek and Latin write separately.

Greek ἀνόμων ('lawless ones', from ἄνομος, lit. 'without law') and Latin iniquis ('the unjust/wicked') describe the malefactors by privation of νόμος/law, whereas the Syriac ܥܘܠܐ (root e-w-l, cognate with Hebrew עוֹל 'iniquity') frames them by positive moral wrongdoing. The quotation derives from Isa 53:12 LXX, and the lexical spread reflects each tradition's standard equivalent for the transgressor word-group.

Greek ἐλογίσθη (aorist passive of λογίζομαι, 'was reckoned/counted') is matched by the Syriac Ethpaal ܐܬܚܫܒ (root kh-sh-b, cognate with Arabic ḥasaba and Hebrew ḥāšab, 'to reckon'), a near-exact semantic equivalent. Latin renders it periphrastically as reputatus est, the standard analytic passive, lengthening one Greek synthetic form into two Latin tokens.

The Clementine Vulgate inserts an explicit colon after dicit to mark the boundary between the citation formula and the quoted scripture (Isa 53:12). Neither the Greek (which uses only a comma after λέγουσα) nor the unpointed Peshitta supplies a corresponding heavy punctuation mark.
